period: New Kingdom, 18th Dynasty, Thutmose IV to Amenhotep III, c. 1400-1350 BC
summary: Two small chapels with some of the most reproduced images of Egyptian daily life: musicians, harvests, and a cat with a fish under the chair.
look: Two separate small tombs a short walk apart. Nakht's is a single painted hall: the banquet on the south part of the west wall, fishing and fowling on its north part, the farming scenes on the east wall. Menna's is larger: a broad front hall with the harvest and banquet, then a long hall with the funeral, the weighing of the heart and a marsh hunt.
story:
Nakht was a scribe and 'astronomer of Amun', probably under Thutmose IV, and his wife Tawy appears beside him. In his banquet, women musicians and dancers entertain the couple, among them the famous trio with a double pipe, a lute and a harp, and under a chair a cat eats a fish.

Menna was overseer of fields of Amun and of the king, and his wife was Henuttawy. Recent study suggests most of the painting was done under Amenhotep III. His harvest is full of bureaucracy: men measure the fields with a rope and scribes count the grain. His back hall has one of the earliest painted weighings of the heart. Someone in antiquity gouged out the eyes and faces of Menna and his wife, perhaps a personal enemy.
details: Nakht, west wall, south part: the three women musicians with double pipe, lute and harp.
Nakht's banquet: the cat under the chair, eating a fish.
Menna's front hall: surveyors measuring a field of grain with a rope, while scribes record.
Menna's harvest: look for two girls squabbling in the stubble.
Menna's long hall: the damaged eyes and faces of Menna and Henuttawy.
fun_fact: Menna's job was assessing fields for tax, and his eternal paradise still includes the men with the measuring rope.
narration: Two small tombs, two officials of the same age, and some of the most copied pictures in Egypt. Nakht was a scribe and astronomer of Amun. In his banquet, three young women play a double pipe, a lute and a harp, and under a chair a cat is eating a fish. Menna was an overseer of fields, so his walls are about the harvest: men measure the fields with a rope, scribes count the grain, and two girls squabble in the stubble. In his back hall is one of the earliest painted weighings of the heart. Someone in antiquity scratched out Menna's eyes and his wife's face, perhaps an enemy who wanted him blind in the afterlife. Look for those damaged faces as you go round.

summary: The domed mud-brick house where Howard Carter lived while he cleared Tutankhamun's tomb, with an exact copy of the burial chamber next door.
look: A low mud-brick house with a central dome, on the rise where the road turns into the Valley of the Kings. Inside: his study, bedroom and photographic darkroom, furnished with period pieces and old photographs. Next to it, a separate building holds the full-size facsimile of Tutankhamun's burial chamber.
story:
Howard Carter built this house in 1910 while he was working for Lord Carnarvon, a short ride from the Valley of the Kings. After he found Tutankhamun's tomb in November 1922, he spent nearly ten years clearing and recording it; the main work ran until 1929 and the last until February 1932. Even afterwards he came back to this house in winter. He died in London in 1939.

The house has been restored and opened as a small museum. In 2014 a facsimile of the burial chamber, recorded in fine detail and reproduced by the Madrid studio Factum Arte, opened beside it, to give visitors an alternative to the crowded, fragile original. Every crack and every brown spot of old fungus is there.
details: The central dome over the main room, built to keep the house cool.
The darkroom: photography was central to recording every object from the tomb.
In the replica: the painted walls with Ay performing the Opening of the Mouth.
In the replica: the brown fungus spots, reproduced exactly.
fun_fact: The replica is so exact that it reproduces the damage: the brown fungus spots on the walls were copied as faithfully as the paintings.
narration: This domed mud-brick house was Howard Carter's home on the West Bank. He built it in 1910, a short ride from the Valley of the Kings. After he found Tutankhamun's tomb in November 1922, he spent nearly ten years clearing and recording it, and this is where he came home at night. Inside you can see his study, his bedroom and a darkroom for the photographs. Next door is something unexpected: an exact copy of Tutankhamun's burial chamber, made by the Madrid studio Factum Arte and opened in 2014 to take pressure off the real tomb. In the copy, look for the brown spots on the walls: even the fungus has been reproduced.

period: New Kingdom, 19th Dynasty, Seti I, c. 1290-1279 BC, completed under Ramesses II
summary: The quiet northern end of the line of royal temples: Seti I's house of eternity, with a chapel for his father, who had no time to build one.
look: The courts and pylons are ruined and much of the eastern part lies under the modern village of Qurna, but the inner temple still stands behind its columned portico, with a small hypostyle hall and sanctuaries. One chapel is dedicated to Seti's father, Ramesses I.
story:
Seti I seems to have built this temple late in his reign, and his son Ramesses II probably finished it after his death. Like the other 'mansions of millions of years' along the edge of the fields, it served the cult of the dead king together with Amun of Karnak.

One chapel honours Seti's father, Ramesses I, an old army officer who founded the 19th Dynasty but reigned for less than two years and built no mortuary temple of his own. So the son built one for the father, and the grandson completed it.

The forecourts and pylons are now in ruins, but the inner rooms keep fine reliefs. Few visitors come, which is a large part of the pleasure.
details: The portico: the front of the surviving inner temple, facing the ruined courts.
The chapel of Ramesses I: father and son together, honoured by the grandson.
Cartouches of Seti I beside those of Ramesses II, who completed the work.
The modern village around the ruins, built over the temple's eastern half.
fun_fact: Ramesses I reigned for less than two years, but thanks to his son and grandson he got a chapel here, a tomb in the Valley of the Kings and a mummy that travelled to Niagara Falls and back.
narration: This is the temple of Seti the First, the most northerly of the royal temples along the edge of the fields, and usually the quietest. Seti built it late in his reign as his house of eternity, and his son Ramesses the Second seems to have finished it. Inside, one chapel belongs to Seti's father, Ramesses the First, an old army officer who reigned less than two years and never had time to build a temple of his own. So the son built one for the father, and the grandson completed it. The front courts are ruined and partly buried under the modern village, but the inner rooms keep fine carved reliefs. Look for Seti's cartouches beside those of Ramesses: a family business in stone.

summary: The pyramid-shaped peak over the Valley of the Kings, home of a cobra goddess who punished the tomb builders' sins and forgave them.
look: Find the highest point of the Theban hills: el-Qurn, the Horn, 420 m high, rising above the Valley of the Kings. From the valley entrance it looks almost like a pyramid. The workmen's path from Deir el-Medina climbs its flank to their huts on the pass, and the rock shrine they shared between Meretseger and Ptah lies on the path from the village towards the Valley of the Queens.
story:
Some Egyptologists think the shape of the Qurn helped the New Kingdom kings choose to be buried beneath it: having given up building pyramids, they had a natural one standing over their tombs. The peak was thought to be an entrance to the underworld, sacred to Hathor and above all to Meretseger, 'She Who Loves Silence', the silence of the desert cemetery.

She was a cobra, sometimes with a woman's head, and the special goddess of the Deir el-Medina workmen. They had temptations: copper tools were valuable, and oaths were easy to break. Meretseger struck thieves and oath-breakers with her venom, or with blindness, but forgave those who repented, an idea of sin and forgiveness that is unusual in Egyptian religion.

The draughtsman Neferabu set up a stela, now in Turin, confessing: 'I did the transgression against the Peak, and she taught a lesson to me.' After he begged forgiveness she 'made my malady forgotten', and he warned his colleagues: 'beware the Peak! For there is a lion within her!'

Her rock shrine, shared with Ptah, god of craftsmen, was a row of small caves; earthquakes brought down the vaults, but stelae remain on the walls. When the royal valley fell out of use, her cult faded, around the 11th-10th centuries BC.
details: The summit of el-Qurn: from the Valley of the Kings entrance, its pyramid shape is clearest.
The workmen's path over the hill between Deir el-Medina and the Valley of the Kings.
The rock shrine of Ptah and Meretseger: small caves with stelae cut into the cliff.
Above the shrine: a rock that looks like the head of a snake.
fun_fact: This may be the only Egyptian goddess with a reputation for forgiveness: workmen who confessed their sins to her claimed she healed them.
narration: Look up at the highest peak above the Valley of the Kings. Its name is el-Qurn, the Horn, and it rises 420 metres. From the valley entrance it looks almost like a pyramid, and some Egyptologists think that is one reason the kings chose to be buried beneath it: after giving up building pyramids, they had a natural one standing over their tombs. The Egyptians believed the peak was a door to the underworld, and the home of a goddess called Meretseger, She Who Loves Silence. She was a cobra, sometimes with a woman's head, and the tomb builders of Deir el-Medina took her very seriously. If a workman stole copper tools or broke an oath, she struck him with her venom or with blindness. If he repented, she forgave him. A draughtsman called Neferabu set up a stone, now in Turin, confessing: I did the transgression against the Peak, and she taught a lesson to me. He was healed, and he warned his colleagues: beware the Peak, for there is a lion within her. Find the summit now: it watches over every site on the West Bank.
